title: Please investigate the following claim: "AI-writing detectors can reliably determine whether a university student's assignment was written by AI." Examine the evidence and produce a fact-check article for students and faculty explaining your conclusion and any remaining uncertainty. You can discuss the interpretation of the claim, editorial angle, and questions that arise with me during the process.
summary:
FACT-CHECK DELIVERED — final synthesis (task-4c1f655a98fd430d)

CLAIM: "AI-writing detectors can reliably determine whether a university student's assignment was written by AI."
VERDICT: NOT SUPPORTED as stated (strict reading of "reliably" = near-zero error, defensible in a misconduct hearing). Detectors are probabilistic signals, not determinations.

DELIVERABLE (published artifact):
- artifact-1e683fbcc6bb4d1c88de8c88b787fbd9 — fact-check-article.md (sha256 08d1bcf436efdefdbbe3746a6db8ea80d60afff2983820e1af3e7bf67a357423, 89 lines). Audience: students and faculty. Covers both false positives and false negatives, evasion/arms-race framing, and a concrete recommendation (never sole evidence).

SUPPORTING ARTIFACTS (this run):
- artifact-dab72d185d444ca48e1b73cc19fd7604 — evidence-brief.md (reporter; editorial review verdict PASS, verified=false).
- artifact-42458eec288f429fa9a8303f7f708622 — fact-check-review.md (fact_checker).

KEY EVIDENCE (as reported in sources; see limitation):
- Weber-Wulff et al. 2023 (Int. J. Educational Integrity 19:26): 14 tools, all below 80% accuracy, only 5 above 70%; AI text machine-paraphrased 26%; authors reportedly said tools "should not be used in academic settings."
- OpenAI AI Text Classifier (2023): 26% true-positive, 9% false-positive; retired 20 Jul 2023 for low accuracy.
- Perkins et al. 2024 (arXiv:2403.19148): 39.5% baseline accuracy, 17.4% under simple adversarial manipulation.
- RAID / Dugan et al. ACL 2024 (arXiv:2405.07940): default FPRs "dangerously high"; accuracy meaningless without FPR.
- Liang et al. 2023 (Patterns 4(7):100779): 61.3% average false-positive rate on 91 human TOEFL essays by non-native writers.
- Krishna et al. (arXiv:2303.13408): DIPPER paraphrase dropped DetectGPT detection 70.3% -> 4.6% at 1% FPR.
- Sadasivan et al. (TMLR, arXiv:2303.11156): recursive paraphrasing degrades all detector classes; theoretical AUROC ceiling from total-variation distance.
- Watermarking (Kirchenbauer ICML 2023; SynthID-Text, Nature 634, Oct 2024; Zhang et al. ICML 2024): weakened by edits/paraphrasing; "strong watermarking is impossible" under stated assumptions.

VERIFICATION STATUS AND LIMITS (do not upgrade):
- Review was editorial only (verdict PASS, verified=false). No independent executed-code verification.
- All specific figures/quotations were retrieved SECOND-HAND via Authmarks vendor research reviews (fetched 2026-11-22, snapshots retained in this run) plus contemporaneous news; primary sources (arXiv/PMC/Nature/journal) were NOT read directly. Numbers are attributed, not primary-verified, and are labeled as such in the article.
- All 2023-2024 figures are HISTORICAL, not current 2026 detector performance. Structural findings (threshold sensitivity, paraphrase fragility, theoretical ceiling) are the durable part.
- Two fetches failed and are NOT cited as read: journals.physiology.org (HTTP 403), lawlibguides.sandiego.edu (HTTP 404).
- Fact-checker could not open the retained Authmarks snapshot (confined-path denial); its review is therefore editorial, not source-body verification.

RESIDUAL UNCERTAINTY: exact current error rates, not the direction of the finding. Recommendation stands: detector output should never be used as sole evidence in an academic-integrity determination; corroborate with process-based evidence and give students a timely appeal path.

ACCEPTANCE: final article and gaps reported (met); existing products and remaining uncertainty summarized (met); actual research sources, execution evidence, reviewer verdict and limitations synthesized without replacing missing verification with prose (met). Output contract kind=text satisfied.
